source.title: Toward Inference-optimal Mixture-of-Expert Large Language Models
source.authors: Longfei Yun; Yong-Hao Zhuang; Yao Fu; E. Xing; Hao Zhang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends scaling-law experiments to MoE language models, measuring validation loss across model size, training tokens, and number of experts.
record.gate_note: Section 4–5 inference-cost and budget-comparison results are not included as rows because they do not directly measure the claim versions' power-law loss or parameter/token allocation trends. Results cited from earlier work are not recorded as this study's results.
record.test_reason: The authors train MoE language models (81M–679M dense-equivalent, 4–32 experts) on 2.5B–20B SlimPajama tokens. They fit a power-law-form loss in N, D and E, so their own validation-loss results bear on V1 in a new architecture setting.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that MoE validation loss follows a power-law-form relation in model size, tokens and experts, with saturating returns in experts. They argue inference cost must be added to budget allocation. They find that 4/8-expert MoEs are most serving-efficient at equal quality but cost 2.5–3.5x more training. Over-training smaller 16/32-expert MoEs on more data is recommended under a training budget.
record.recipe_differences: Like prior scaling-law work, it trains a sweep of language models and fits validation-loss relations; it extends the setup to MoE models by varying expert count and fitting a law with an expert-saturation term. The tested models use SlimPajama and are much smaller than the very large runs discussed in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The proposed law includes an expert-count saturation threshold; the paper reports diminishing returns at higher expert counts. It does not report sensitivity to alternative fitting methods or fitting choices.

fits_no_version.finding: The validation-loss gain from more experts diminishes and saturates; going from 16 to 32 experts gives a smaller benefit.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In MoE LMs, loss falls roughly as a power of expert count, with saturation at a threshold Emax.

record.problems: The scaling sweep is limited to 100 million–730 million dense-model parameters and 2.5B–20B training tokens. The paper reports fit-error metrics but no confidence intervals or error bars for the scaling observations. It does not test extrapolation on held-out, much larger runs.
record.rows_left_out: Inference-cost profiling and budget-allocation comparisons in Sections 4–5 and Figures 2–6 were left out because they do not directly report the power-law loss or parameter/token growth measures named by the tested version.

untested.parts: Power law over several orders of magnitude: N spans about 8x and D 8x; dense-only scaling is not reported separately.
The fitted law is applied to budgets of 1e21–8e21 FLOPs (about 3–6B dense) in Sec 5, but those predictions are never checked against trained runs.
Loss-optimal N and D are derived from the fitted law, not measured. No fitted growth exponents for Nopt and Dopt are reported.
Only one fitting procedure is used; no comparison of fitting choices.

missing.what: Fitted values of the exponents α, β, γ and the constants of Eq. 4 are not reported. A researcher would need them to compare with the Kaplan and Chinchilla exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V1 limits_scope label was dropped: the narrow N/D range is an untested part, not a qualification shown by results. The Sec 5 budget-allocation numbers are model-based extrapolations from the fitted law to about 100x the training compute, not measured runs. They do not count as tests of V2 or V3.

versions.untested_parts: The reported sweeps do not cover several orders of magnitude in model size or training tokens, and the paper does not test dense-model scaling.
The paper reports fit quality on its experimental sweep, but does not fit on small runs and test predictions on runs orders of magnitude larger.
The paper considers loss-optimal configurations under budgets, but does not report fitted power-law growth of optimal parameter and token counts with compute.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, repeated-data, fine-tuning, or transfer setting is tested.
No downstream task performance is measured.
The paper specifies one fitting procedure and reports one fit; it does not compare fitting choices or test whether exponents or optimal allocations change with those choices.

rows.subject: MoE model sweep
rows.size_stated: dense model size ranging from 100 million to 730 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Swept model size and measured validation loss across MoE runs.
rows.measure: validation loss as model size varies
rows.value: The paper reports parallel lines for different dense model sizes, with a consistent slope across sizes.
rows.note: Qualitative description of the experimental sweep; no per-model loss values are given in the text.
rows.check: Value is qualitative only ('parallel lines… consistent slope', Sec 3.2/Fig 1); no per-run losses are given. The model-size range is under one order of magnitude (81M–679M non-embedding).

rows.subject: MoE model sweep
rows.size_stated: dense model size ranging from 100 million to 730 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Swept the number of training tokens and measured validation loss.
rows.measure: validation loss as training-token count varies
rows.value: The paper reports a consistent slope across different training-token counts, with lines differing mainly in their intercepts.
rows.note: The authors also state that dataset size conforms to a power-law relationship with validation loss.
rows.check: Qualitative only. The token range is 2.5B–20B, under one order of magnitude.

rows.subject: MoE model sweep
rows.size_stated: dense model size ranging from 100 million to 730 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Fit the proposed scaling law to experimental runs varying model size, tokens, and expert count.
rows.measure: fit error for validation loss (RMSLE and Huber loss)
rows.note: The authors say the fitted validation loss closely mirrors the actual validation loss.
rows.check: In-sample goodness of fit (RMSLE 3.908e-3) on the same runs used for fitting. It shows the power-law form fits but is not a prediction on held-out runs.

rows.subject: MoE model sweep
rows.size_stated: dense model size ranging from 100 million to 730 million parameters
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of experts and measured validation loss.
rows.measure: validation loss as expert count varies
rows.value: The paper reports a roughly power-law benefit from increasing experts over part of the range, diminishing returns as expert count increases, and saturation at a threshold; the 16-to-32 increase shows diminishing benefit.
rows.note: This is a finding about expert count and saturation, which is not directly named by the listed claim versions.
rows.check: Expert-count saturation is not a version's measure. Correctly unlinked and recorded under fits_no_version.

relationships.condition: MoE LMs, 81M–679M dense-equivalent params, 2.5B–20B tokens, 4–32 experts
relationships.reason: The authors report consistent power-law slopes in N and D across settings (r1, r2), and their law fits with RMSLE 3.9e-3 (r3).
relationships.display_finding: Parameter and token power-law slopes remained consistent across settings, and the fitted law achieved RMSLE of 3.9×10^−3.

relation.reason: Its measured validation losses and fitted scaling relation directly bear on V1.

tranche.reason: The study extends language-model loss scaling to an MoE setting and reports its own training sweep and fitted loss relation.

source_check.notes: Both parameter and token sweeps span less than one order of magnitude. The reported fit errors use the fitting runs; they do not establish extrapolation to larger held-out runs.

statements.correction: Section 3.2 reports parallel expert-count curves across dense model sizes and training-token settings. Equation 4 includes power-law terms in model size and tokens, expert saturation, and a model-size/expert interaction. Appendix D reports in-sample RMSLE 3.908e-3. The sweep covers approximately 81M–679M non-embedding dense-equivalent parameters and 2.5B–20B tokens.
statements.problem: The slope description conflates expert-count scaling across model sizes and token counts with separately measured parameter/data slopes.

reader_labels.label: supports

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The tested ranges are 100 million to 730 million parameters and 2.5B to 20B tokens, not several orders of magnitude; this study therefore does not establish the full stated range (r1, r2).
